opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that concern comes from a misunderstanding of where the learning actually happens. The reward is not the only signal the agent learns from. It's the thing that defines what the agent is *for*, its goal, but most of what the agent learns comes from everything else in its experience.

Think about an animal, or a person. You get reward relatively rarely, and it's a single number. But every moment you're getting this enormous stream of sensation. You take an action and something happens. You can learn from that. You can learn to predict what will happen next, you can learn a model of the world, how it responds to what you do. That's where the bulk of the information is. It's in the transitions, in the predictions, not in the scalar reward.

And then there's temporal difference learning, which is really the key idea here. You don't have to wait for the final outcome to learn. If you're playing chess and you make a move and suddenly you realize your position has gotten much worse, you learn from that right away. Your value function changes, and that change is itself a learning signal. So the sparse reward gets turned into a dense signal by learning predictions of it. The value function bootstraps from itself, step by step.

So I'd say the right picture is: the agent has a goal, given by reward, but it also has a world model, it has many predictions, maybe it has subgoals and options, ways of behaving that it's learned along the way. All of those are learned from the rich stream of experience. The reward just tells you what matters in the end. It's sufficient to define the problem. It doesn't have to carry all the information. That's the whole point of having a mind that learns from experience: you extract far more from the world than the world explicitly tells you.

r001.rationale: The response says most learning comes from the agent’s broader experience, including transitions, sensations, and predictions, rather than solely from reward.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that concern gets things backwards. The reward is the goal, it's not the information source. Nobody ever said all the learning has to come from the reward signal. The world is giving you an enormous flow of information every moment, the whole sensory stream, everything you observe, and the question of what you do with it is a question about how you build your representations and your model of the world. Reward just tells you which way is up.

So when people say reward is too sparse, too low-bandwidth, I'd say, yes, of course it is, if you imagine learning everything by trial and error on a scalar. But that's not what a reinforcement learning agent has to do. You have prediction. You can predict all kinds of things about your sensory input, about what will happen if you take various actions, and those predictions are checked against experience every single step. That's where the bandwidth is. Temporal difference learning, general value functions, learning a model of the world, these are all ways of extracting knowledge from experience without any reward being involved at all. Then the reward comes in to tell you which of those things you've learned matter, which to pursue.

I'd actually go further and say the reward being simple is a virtue. It's what lets you have a clean statement of the problem. A single number, maximize it over time, and everything else is a means to that end. If you try to make the reward carry all the information, you end up with the supervised learning view where someone has to tell the agent what to do, and that's exactly what doesn't scale. The point of reinforcement learning is that the agent figures it out from its own experience. The reward is thin on purpose. The richness comes from the world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says learning can use the full sensory stream and predictions checked against ongoing experience, rather than relying solely on the reward signal.

astra-6.text:
I think that concern confuses two different things: where we get our knowledge and how we decide what to do. Reward doesn't have to provide all the information we learn from. The stream of observations provides an enormous amount of information. You can learn how the world works, predict what will happen next, and learn the consequences of your actions without waiting for a reward.

The reward tells you what matters. If you learn a model of the world, you can then use that model to work out which actions will lead to more reward. You don't need the reward signal to separately teach you every fact that goes into that decision.

Now, sparse reward can certainly make a particular learning problem difficult. You may have to explore for a long time before you discover anything useful. But that's different from saying that reward has to carry all the information needed for intelligence. Reinforcement learning doesn't mean that everything you learn is a prediction of reward. It means that the knowledge you acquire ultimately helps you choose actions to achieve your goal.

r001.rationale: The response says observations provide substantial information for learning about the world and action consequences, without relying solely on reward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that concern confuses two different things: where the goal comes from and where the information for learning comes from. Reward tells you what you’re trying to achieve. It doesn’t have to tell you everything about how the world works.

An agent has this enormous stream of observations and actions. It can learn to predict what it will see next, what will happen if it takes a particular action, and how different parts of its experience relate to one another. None of that requires a new reward on every step. But ultimately, you want that knowledge to help you get more reward.

So I wouldn’t say that all learning has to be driven directly by reward. You can learn a model of the world, and then use that model to plan. The reward specifies which outcomes you prefer; experience tells you how to get to them.

There’s still a real problem when rewards are delayed or rare. How do you explore? How do you assign credit to something you did a long time ago? Those are important research problems. But the fact that the reward signal is small doesn’t mean the agent has only a small amount of information to learn from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents can learn from their stream of observations and actions, including predicting outcomes and learning a world model, without needing a new reward at every step. It distinguishes this experience-based learning from reward’s role in specifying goals.
